articles.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan to become first Muslim senator in US history
articles.summary: El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in US history.
articles.content:
The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.

The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.

El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.

Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all."

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country.

The issue carries particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US.

It also fuelled tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, whose primary campaign received millions of dollars in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).

The contest was widely seen as a test of the political influence of the Democratic left in a key battleground state, following a series of primary wins by democratic socialist candidates in more politically favoured districts.

El-Sayed thanked the crowd in the early hours of Wednesday morning for taking a chance on "the unlikeliest of candidates", saying his win was theirs. He told the crowd the campaign against him had been one of the ugliest seen in their lifetime.

The impact is broad, affecting societal inclusion and political representation, and the article provides sufficient context about the campaign and its significance.

articles.title: Fleabag star offers rent-free flat to new writers
articles.summary: Phoebe Waller-Bridge is donating the accommodation to playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds.
articles.content:
Fleabag creator, writer and actress Phoebe Waller-Bridge is offering a rent-free flat in London for writers early in their careers.

The 41-year-old has bought and donated the flat as part of a new theatre initiative Writers' Block, which aims to address the cost of London accommodation for playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds.

She bought the flat specifically for writers who are starting out and are struggling to afford accommodation in the capital, and has donated its use alongside what the scheme called a "generous financial contribution".

Her flat will be provided without rent, with the resident paying bills only.

Adolescence co-creator Jack Thorne – who wrote the films Wonder and Enola Holmes, as well as the Harry Potter And The Cursed Child stage play – is also providing financial backing to the scheme.

"I was lucky when I started out, my brother lived in Croydon and was able to put me up," he said.

"He did so, rather selflessly, for five years, before I moved to Luton and he got his peace.

"For many writers, the need for a roof makes writing impossible which is why this pilot is so important. If we want stories told about our complicated world, we need writers of every background writing them.

"If you're from privilege, your biggest problem is what to fill a page with. If you're not, so much of your struggle is about the need to survive."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a tangible, inspiring initiative addressing socioeconomic barriers for underprivileged playwrights by providing rent-free accommodation in London, enabling creative work and promoting diversity in storytelling. The impact is meaningful for a broad group of emerging writers facing financial hardship, with clear context and support from notable figures.

articles.title: Chinese doctoral students in clinical medicine can graduate without a thesis — more degrees to follow
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03480-7Postgraduate students studying professional medicine degrees can qualify with a ‘practical achievement’.
articles.content:
Postgraduate students studying clinical medicine in China have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case, rather than a thesis.Credit: Xie Shangguo/VCG via Getty

Master’s and doctoral candidates in some clinical medicine degrees in China can now graduate with a ‘practical achievement’ instead of a thesis. This is the second field to open such a pathway. Since 2024, master’s and PhD students in engineering have been allowed to graduate from universities across China after developing a new product, technique, project or installation.

On 22 October, a team of government-appointed education advisers released draft policy documents setting out the rules for the graduation pathway for students pursuing a professional master’s or doctoral degree in clinical medicine — both are three-year courses typically taken by medical graduates and practising physicians.

In China, professional postgraduate courses focus on training students to solve problems in a particular line of work rather than developing research skills, as they would in an academic degree. The rules state that students have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case or an investigation into a problem facing medical institutes.

Postgraduate courses in translation, agriculture, accounting and arts are expected to introduce similar pathways to graduation, according to China’s Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council, a government body driving reforms for postgraduate education.

These reforms are a step in the right direction, because students preparing for professional careers should be trained and assessed in ways that reflect those careers, says Futao Huang, a researcher of higher-education policy at Hiroshima University in Higashihiroshima, Japan. “The real challenge is to develop credible, transparent and profession-specific standards for assessing practical achievements,” Huang adds.

Real-life problems

For students pursuing a professional degree in clinical medicine, the new graduation pathway means that they can be assessed on the contribution that their research will bring to patients and society, says Zhou Feifei, a spinal surgeon at Peking University Third Hospital in Beijing. “This will encourage them to find problems in real life and to address the problem using a scientific way,” he adds.

One of Zhou’s students, Tie Dazhao, was the first person to graduate with a ‘practical PhD’ in clinical medicine in June, having been selected as a pilot case in 2023. Tie developed an artificial-intelligence-empowered software programme that can help physicians to classify a type of rare spinal condition and recommend suitable treatment strategies to them, says Zhou.

Individual universities are encouraged to form their own policies on training practical postgraduate students and what requirements students must meet to graduate, says Liping Duan, chief physician of gastroenterology at Peking University Third Hospital and a member of a national advisory committee tasked with formulating the policy for clinical medicine. One of the biggest challenges will be creating a uniform standard to assess practical achievements, Duan says. “What works for cardiology may not work for dermatology, for example,” she adds.

How to control the quality of the achievements will also be important, Duan says. “Some people may mistakenly think that graduation has become easier now that students can choose not to write a thesis.”
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant education reform in China allowing clinical medicine postgraduate students to graduate based on practical achievements rather than traditional theses. This change promotes career-relevant training, encourages real-world problem solving in healthcare, and may improve medical practice and patient outcomes. The reform has broad societal impact by potentially enhancing healthcare education and delivery, and it reflects a meaningful policy shift with detailed context and examples.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À partir de 2026, les étudiants en médecine clinique en Chine peuvent désormais obtenir leur diplôme en réalisant un travail pratique, comme l’analyse d’un cas médical spécial ou la résolution d’un problème hospitalier, au lieu d’une thèse traditionnelle. articles.title: Gender equality pays off for business – so why are companies pulling back?
articles.summary: Gender equality and diversity are good for business – but while increasing numbers of women are reaching top spots in the corporate world, more initiatives are needed to keep momentum going.
articles.content:
The recommendation comes from the International Labour Organization (ILO) in its report Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success, published on Tuesday.

Between 2013 and 2025, the share of companies with a woman board chair rose from 13.1 per cent to 30.1 per cent. The share with a woman CEO climbed from 23.5 per cent to 28.2 per cent.

Yet women remain under-represented in management overall, occupying around a third of managerial-level roles. Gender balance increased at senior and top management levels during the same period but declined at junior and middle management.

Commitment vs execution

The report draws on a 2025 ILO survey of 11,957 enterprises in 99 countries, as well as surveys conducted in 2013 and 2018, 30 years of labour market data, secondary research and case studies.

Tweet URL

Nearly 70 per cent of enterprises surveyed in 2025 said gender equality and diversity initiatives had improved business outcomes, up more than 11 percentage points from 2018.

Among those reporting increased profits through initiatives promoting women in management, 87.4 per cent reported gains of at least five per cent. Firms with women CEOs and board chairs were also more likely to report better business outcomes.

Still, although nearly three quarters (74.8 per cent) of enterprises reported having a gender equality and diversity policy or equivalent in place in 2025, the share that implemented them stood at 26.5 per cent, down from 37.4 per cent in 2018.

“The decline included measures that enterprises themselves identified as among the most effective, including maternity leave and support programmes and equal pay initiatives,” the ILO said.

Making the case

The UN agency noted that the findings come despite major advances in women’s education, including greater enrolment in tertiary education when compared to men.

Yet women continue to be under-represented in some of the business functions and sectors that can pave a path to senior leadership.

“At a time when enterprises are competing for skills and talent, leaving women’s potential untapped makes little business sense,” said Maria Paz Anzorreguy, Director of the ILO Bureau for Employers’ Activities.

A future where women ‘shine’

The report outlines practical measures, including strengthening women’s leadership pipelines, improving access to roles and sectors where women remain under-represented, and using gender metrics and voluntary targets.

It also calls for addressing structural barriers outside the workplace, including unequal care responsibilities, occupational segregation and persistent social norms.

Rosemarie P. Rafael, founder and chairperson of Philippines-based logistics company Airspeed – among three case studies included in the report – shared her perspective with the authors.

“A company with a nurturing culture, with fair recruitment, promotion, and remuneration, will get the best talent, both women and men,” she said.

“And when women know they have a future in the company, they shine.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant and positive real-world impact: gender equality initiatives in business improve outcomes and representation of women in leadership, supported by comprehensive data from the ILO. It highlights meaningful progress and ongoing challenges, offering practical solutions with broad societal relevance beyond a niche audience.
articles.personality_title: Gender equality boosts business success but efforts are slowing down
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The International Labour Organization (ILO) studied how gender equality affects businesses. Their report looked at data from 2013 to 2025, including surveys of almost 12,000 companies in 99 countries.

**What happened** – The report shows more women are reaching top company roles. The number of companies with a woman as board chair rose from 13.1% in 2013 to 30.1% in 2025. Women CEOs increased from 23.5% to 28.2%. Still, women hold about one-third of all management jobs, with fewer in junior and middle roles.

**Impact** – Companies with gender equality programs report better business results. Nearly 70% said these initiatives helped improve outcomes, and 87.4% of those saw profits grow by at least 5%. Women leaders often lead to stronger companies. However, fewer companies are actually putting these equality policies into action now compared to 2018, including important measures like maternity leave and equal pay.

**What's next step** – The report suggests companies need to do more to support women’s leadership by removing barriers like unequal care duties and social norms. It encourages clear goals and tracking progress. Businesses that create fair and supportive environments can attract and keep talented women who will help the company succeed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – While gender equality in business improves performance and leadership diversity, more action is needed to maintain progress and fully unlock women’s potential.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’égalité des sexes stimule la réussite des entreprises mais les efforts ralentissent
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Organisation internationale du travail (OIT) a étudié l’impact de l’égalité des sexes dans les entreprises. Son rapport analyse des données de 2013 à 2025, incluant des enquêtes auprès de près de 12 000 entreprises dans 99 pays.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le rapport montre que de plus en plus de femmes accèdent à des postes de direction. La part des entreprises avec une femme présidente du conseil d’administration est passée de 13,1 % en 2013 à 30,1 % en 2025. Les femmes PDG sont passées de 23,5 % à 28,2 %. Pourtant, les femmes occupent environ un tiers des postes de gestion, avec moins de présence aux niveaux junior et intermédiaire.

**Impact** – Les entreprises avec des programmes d’égalité des sexes constatent de meilleurs résultats. Près de 70 % disent que ces initiatives ont amélioré leurs performances, et 87,4 % de celles-ci ont vu leurs bénéfices augmenter d’au moins 5 %. Les femmes dirigeantes renforcent souvent les entreprises. Cependant, moins d’entreprises mettent en œuvre ces politiques aujourd’hui qu’en 2018, notamment des mesures importantes comme le congé maternité et l’égalité salariale.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le rapport recommande aux entreprises d’en faire plus pour soutenir le leadership des femmes en supprimant les obstacles comme les responsabilités familiales inégales et les normes sociales. Il encourage à fixer des objectifs clairs et à suivre les progrès. Les entreprises qui créent un environnement juste et favorable peuvent attirer et retenir des femmes talentueuses qui aideront leur succès.

**Une phrase clé** – Bien que l’égalité des sexes améliore la performance et la diversité des dirigeants, il faut plus d’actions pour maintenir les progrès et révéler pleinement le potentiel des femmes.
articles.personality_title_es: La igualdad de género impulsa el éxito empresarial pero los esfuerzos disminuyen
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Organización Internacional del Trabajo (OIT) estudió cómo la igualdad de género afecta a las empresas. Su informe analiza datos de 2013 a 2025, incluyendo encuestas a casi 12,000 empresas en 99 países.

**Qué pasó** – El informe muestra que más mujeres llegan a cargos altos en las empresas. La proporción de empresas con una mujer como presidenta del consejo aumentó del 13.1% en 2013 al 30.1% en 2025. Las mujeres directoras ejecutivas subieron del 23.5% al 28.2%. Aún así, las mujeres ocupan cerca de un tercio de los puestos gerenciales, con menos presencia en niveles junior y medio.

**Impacto** – Las empresas con programas de igualdad de género reportan mejores resultados. Casi el 70% dijo que estas iniciativas mejoraron sus resultados, y el 87.4% de ellas vio un aumento de ganancias de al menos 5%. Las mujeres líderes suelen fortalecer las empresas. Sin embargo, menos empresas están aplicando estas políticas ahora que en 2018, incluyendo medidas importantes como licencias de maternidad y pago igualitario.

**Próximos pasos** – El informe sugiere que las empresas deben hacer más para apoyar el liderazgo femenino eliminando barreras como las responsabilidades desiguales del cuidado y normas sociales. Recomienda establecer metas claras y medir el progreso. Las empresas que crean ambientes justos y de apoyo pueden atraer y mantener mujeres talentosas que ayudarán al éxito.

**Una frase clave** – Aunque la igualdad de género mejora el desempeño y la diversidad en liderazgo, se necesita más acción para mantener el progreso y aprovechar todo el potencial de las mujeres.
